roles.name: Map Keeper
roles.job: You ask questions, draw a simple map on paper and write one date or reason next to each place.

steps: Each reader reads only his or her chapters and then closes the book.
The Map Keeper asks each reader: “Which places does your part name? What happened there, and when?”

Each reader answers with one sentence from the book, for example: “80 km northeast of Sivas” or “the Mongol state centred in Iran”. The Map Keeper adds the place and the date to the paper map. Places that are farther east, like Turkestan and Khorasan, get an arrow at the edge of the paper.
Together, check your paper map against the map page “Anatolia in Yunus Emre’s Time” in the app and correct anything you placed wrongly.
groupTask.share: Each group shows its map and tells the events in order from 1242 to 1308, using linking words such as “because of”, “However”, “caused” and “Thus”.
groupTask.solo: Cover Chapters 4–7, draw a simple map of Anatolia from memory with the places and dates from the book, then check it on the map page “Anatolia in Yunus Emre’s Time”.

pages.title: Tawhid and Unity
pages.content:
In his poems, he expresses a vivid love for Allah as a way of life, along with fear of Allah and loyalty to the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh).

One of the most important ideas in his works is Tawhid, which means the Oneness of Allah. According to Yunus Emre, Allah, the Creator, is the source of all things. So everything is connected to Him. The Creator is the true and only reality. According to the theory of the unity of existence, which was a key idea for Yunus Emre, there is only one true existence in the universe, and that is Allah.

Yunus says:

[POEM]
English:
“The entire universe is Tawhid; Adam is the one who knows Tawhid.
Whoever denies this Tawhid is an enemy to his own soul.”
Turkish:
Tevhîd imiş cümle âlem, tevhîdi bilendir Âdem
Bu tevhîdi inkâr iden öz cânına düşmânımış
[/POEM]

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
Strong support and faithfulness to someone.
The quality of being single, without any partner or equal.
Joined or linked to something else.
Everything that Allah created, including the earth, the sky and all the stars.
The Sufi idea that only Allah truly exists.
Any person who.

hotspots.title: Tawhid
hotspots.description: Tawhid means the Oneness of Allah, a basic principle in his works.

hotspots.title: Unity
hotspots.description: For Yunus, Allah is the source of all things and the only true reality.

exercises.title: Tawhid
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false? Use Chapter 8.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 8, Yunus Emre believed that every created thing is a true reality on its own, separate from Allah.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8 says that Allah, the Creator, “is the source of all things. So everything is connected to Him. The Creator is the true and only reality.”

feedback.correct: Correct. For Yunus Emre, nothing is separate from Allah: Everything is connected to Him, and He is the only true reality.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 8 again. What does it say about how all things are connected to the Creator?

languageFocusExercises.title: What Do These Phrases Mean?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each phrase from Chapter 8 with its meaning in plain English.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do these phrases from Chapter 8 mean?

matchingPairs.right: a strong and lively feeling
where everything comes from

matchingPairs.left: a key idea for Yunus Emre
matchingPairs.right: a central belief in his thinking

matchingPairs.left: an enemy to his own soul
matchingPairs.right: someone who harms himself

correctAnswer.a key idea for Yunus Emre: a central belief in his thinking

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Vivid” describes something strong and full of life. A “source” is where something begins or comes from. A “key” idea is the most important one, the idea that opens the others. In the poem, a person who is “an enemy to his own soul” is harming himself, not someone else.

feedback.correct: Good. You understood the key phrases of the chapter and the poem.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 8 and the poem again. Ask which phrase is about a feeling, which is about an origin, which is about importance, and which is about harm.

languageFocusExercises.title: Define, Report, Conclude
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 8 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which word fits each gap?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: One of the most important ideas in his works is Tawhid, [blank] means the Oneness of Allah. [blank] Yunus Emre, Allah, the Creator, is the source of all things. [blank] everything is connected to Him.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “…, which means …” adds a definition to a word or idea; “who” is only for people. “According to + person” shows whose view the writer is reporting; “due to” gives a reason, not a viewpoint. “So” draws a conclusion from the idea before it: If Allah is the source of all things, then everything is connected to Him. “But” would show a contrast that is not there.

feedback.correct: Well done. You defined the idea, reported the view and drew the conclusion.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 8 again. Which blank gives a definition, which names whose view it is, and which draws a conclusion?

languageFocusExercises.title: Only One: Say It Another Way
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say that there is only one true reality?

transformItems.source: The Creator is the true and only reality.
transformItems.frame: Nothing is truly real [blank] the Creator.

transformItems.source: … there is only one true existence in the universe, and that is Allah.
transformItems.frame: Allah is [blank] true existence in the universe.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “There is only one …, and that is …” first limits the possibilities to one, then names it. The same idea can be said with “the only …” (Allah is the only true existence) or negatively with “nothing … except / other than …”. All these patterns single out one thing and leave out everything else.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the “only one” meaning in a new structure.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the last sentence before the poem in Chapter 8. It limits the choice to one and then names it. In the first frame, which word means “and nothing else”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Explain an Idea from Definition to Conclusion
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say five or six sentences about an important idea, for example fair play.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does the idea mean, and why does it matter?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Useful language from the chapter includes “the idea of ... which means ...”, “according to ...”, “..., which is/was ...”, “so ...”, “there is only one ..., and that is ...”, and “whoever ...”.

feedback.correct: Keep the paragraph connected: Define the idea first, develop it, then move to a consequence or general statement.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Explain the idea: “… is …, which means …”
discussionPrompts.example: An important idea in sport is fair play, which means respecting the rules and the other team.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Give a view: “According to …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: According to my coach, fair play is more important than winning.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Add information: “This idea, which …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: This idea, which is taught in many sports clubs, helps young players control their anger.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Give a result: “So …”
discussionPrompts.example: So players who respect fair play enjoy the game more.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 5–6 — End: “There is only one …, and that is …” or “Whoever …”
discussionPrompts.example: There is only one real winner in a fair game, and that is the sport itself. Whoever cheats loses the respect of others.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: Besides love for Allah, what does Yunus express in his poems?
options: fear of Allah and loyalty to the Prophet (pbuh)
beforeYouRead.quote: along with fear of Allah and loyalty to the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh)

iCan: I can explain the idea of Tawhid in simple words.
I can define an idea and say whose view it is.
I can explain an important idea from definition to conclusion.

pages.title: Allah’s Commands
pages.content:
As a result of creation, the original unity was lost and multiplicity appeared. All creations in the world are just reflections of Allah’s names. In this way, every creature is an image, but only Allah is truly real. The main goal for humans is to reach unity with Allah.

His words remind us of Allah’s commands for achieving this unity.

Yunus says:

[POEM compact]
English:
“Anyone who claims to be a Muslim should know the requirements of Islam,
He should follow Allah’s command and pray the five daily prayers”
Turkish:
Müslümanım diyen kişi şartı nedir bilse gerek
Tanrı'nın buyruğun tutup beş vakit namaz kılsa gerek
[/POEM]

Love is a very important theme in Yunus Emre’s works. It is the most important part of his philosophy. Those who love the Creator love the created, and those who love the created also love the Creator.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
Things that show or represent something else.
Says that something is true, often without proof.
Things that are necessary or must be done.
The acts of worship that Muslims must perform at set times from dawn to night: Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib and Isha.
Being one.

hotspots.title: A Muslim’s Duties
hotspots.description: The poem says a Muslim should follow Allah’s command and pray the five daily prayers.

hotspots.title: Love
hotspots.description: Love of the Creator and love of His creatures go together.

exercises.title: Unity, Worship and Love
exercises.instructions: Match each idea with what Chapter 9 says about it.
exercises.question: What does Chapter 9 say about each idea?

matchingPairs.right: to reach unity with Allah
an image that reflects Allah’s names

matchingPairs.left: Anyone who claims to be a Muslim
matchingPairs.right: should follow Allah’s command and pray five times a day
the most important part of Yunus Emre’s philosophy

correctAnswer.Every creature: an image that reflects Allah’s names
correctAnswer.Anyone who claims to be a Muslim: should follow Allah’s command and pray five times a day
correctAnswer.Love: the most important part of Yunus Emre’s philosophy

exercises.explanation: Chapter 9 says “The main goal for humans is to reach unity with Allah” and “every creature is an image” of Allah’s names. The poem says a Muslim “should follow Allah’s command and pray the five daily prayers,” and love “is the most important part of his philosophy.”

feedback.correct: Great. You connected the goal of unity with worship and with love.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 9 again from the beginning to the end: The first paragraph, the poem and the last paragraph each explain one or two of these ideas.

languageFocusExercises.title: Follow the Chain of Ideas
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put the sentences from Chapter 9 in order. The linking words can help.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does each idea lead to the next?

sequencingItems.text: In this way, every creature is an image, but only Allah is truly real.
Yunus Emre’s words remind us of Allah’s commands for achieving this unity.
As a result of creation, the original unity lost its unity and multiple existence appeared.
The main goal for humans is to reach unity with Allah.
All creations in the world are just reflections of Allah’s names.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “As a result of + noun” opens the explanation with a cause (creation) and its result. “In this way” points back to the idea just before it (creations are reflections), so it must follow that sentence. “The main goal … is to + verb” states an aim, and “this unity” in the last sentence points back to that aim. “For + -ing” (for achieving) shows purpose, and “remind us of” brings something important back to mind.

feedback.correct: Correct. You used the linking words to rebuild the chain from result to goal to purpose.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the words that point back: “In this way” needs an idea before it, and “this unity” needs a unity that was already mentioned. Then check Chapter 9.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “Should” Mean in the Poem?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the lines of the poem in Chapter 9. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Anyone who claims to be a Muslim should know the requirements of Islam, / He should follow Allah’s command and pray the five daily prayers” What does “should” express in these lines?
options: a guess that the person probably knows it already
something that the person did in the past
a duty that is expected of every person in this group
a wish that the person may or may not have
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Anyone who …” means every person who fits the description, not one particular person. “Should + base verb” here expresses what is expected of that person: a duty or responsibility. In other contexts, “should” can also be a guess (“He should be home by now”), but the poem is about what a person is expected to know and do.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Anyone who … should …” states what is expected of every person in the group.
feedback.incorrect: Read the lines again. Is the poem guessing, telling a story about the past, or saying what a person who claims to be a Muslim is expected to do?

languageFocusExercises.title: Find and Fix the Mistake
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about love?

errorItems.sentence: Love is a very important theme in Yunus Emre’s works. It is most important part of his philosophy.
Those who love the Creator love the created, and those who love the created love also the Creator.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A superlative after a verb needs “the”: “It is the most important part”. It shows that love is above every other part of his philosophy. “Those who + verb” means “the people who …”, so the verb is plural (love). “Also” normally comes before the main verb: “… also love the Creator”. The two halves use the same pattern in reverse, which shows a relationship that works in both directions.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the superlative and kept the two halves balanced.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 9 again. What small word comes before “most important”? Where does “also” go: Before or after the verb?

languageFocusExercises.title: Explain a Goal and the Responsibilities Around It
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say five or six sentences about a goal at school or at home.
languageFocusExercises.question: What is the goal, and what should people do?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Useful language from the chapter includes “as a result of...”, “in this way...”, “the main goal is to...”, “for achieving...”, “remind us of...”, “anyone who... should...”, and “those who..., and those who... also...”.

feedback.correct: Keep the paragraph connected: Establish the situation, state the goal, explain what helps achieve it, and end with a broader responsibility or relationship.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give the situation: “As a result of …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: As a result of a new recycling project, our school now has recycling bins in every classroom.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Add the effect: “In this way, …”
discussionPrompts.example: In this way, students see every day how much paper they use.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Give the goal: “The main goal is to …”
discussionPrompts.example: The main goal is to reduce the school’s waste by half this year.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Give a reminder: “… remind us of …”
discussionPrompts.example: Posters in the corridors remind us of our part in achieving this goal.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 5–6 — End: “Anyone who … should …” and “Those who …, and those who … also …”
discussionPrompts.example: Anyone who uses paper in class should put it in the blue bin. Those who care for the school care for the planet, and those who care for the planet also care for the school.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What appeared when the original unity was lost?
beforeYouRead.quote: the original unity was lost and multiplicity appeared

iCan: I can explain the main goal and the duties named in the chapter.
I can say what is expected of everyone in a group.
I can write about a goal and the responsibilities around it.

pages.title: The Heart and Love
pages.content:
Love brings unity and harmony. According to him, where there is no love, bad feelings such as anger, heartbreak and separation appear.

In Yunus Emre’s philosophy, the heart is the center of love. It is “the throne of the Lord,” that is, the place where Allah reveals Himself. For this reason, he described breaking a heart as destroying Allah’s house. He says:

[POEM]
English:
“The heart is the throne of the Lord, and He looked at it;
Whoever destroys the heart is unfortunate in both worlds.”
Turkish:
Gönül Çalab’ın tahtı, Çalap gönüle baktı;
İki cihan bedbahtı, kim gönül yıkar ise.
[/POEM]

The heart is the eye that sees the truth and the center of understanding.

Yunus Emre emphasizes not only the heart but also the intellect as a value; he described it as “a light from Allah that has existed since eternity.”

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
A peaceful state in which things work well together.
Deep emotional sadness or pain.
The special seat of a king or queen, a sign of power.
The ability to think, understand, and reason.

hotspots.title: The Heart
hotspots.description: The heart is the center of love and understanding, “the throne of the Lord.”

hotspots.title: Intellect
hotspots.description: Yunus also valued the intellect as “a light from Allah.”

exercises.title: Allah’s House
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the best answer from Chapter 10.
exercises.question: Why did Yunus Emre describe breaking a heart as destroying Allah’s house?
options: Because the intellect is a light from Allah that has existed since eternity.
Because the heart is the center of anger, heartbreak and separation.
Because the heart is the throne of the Lord, where Allah reveals Himself.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 10 says the heart is “the throne of the Lord,” that is, “the place where Allah reveals Himself. For this reason, he described breaking a heart as destroying Allah’s house.” Anger, heartbreak and separation appear “where there is no love.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The heart is where Allah reveals Himself, so breaking someone’s heart is very serious. This teaches us to treat people’s feelings with respect.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 10 and find the words “For this reason …”. What does the sentence just before them say about the heart?

languageFocusExercises.title: What Do These Phrases Mean?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each phrase from Chapter 10 with its meaning in plain English.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do these phrases from Chapter 10 mean?

matchingPairs.right: the place where Allah reveals Himself
hurting someone deeply
unhappy in this life and the next
with no beginning in time

correctAnswer.the throne of the Lord: the place where Allah reveals Himself
correctAnswer.unfortunate in both worlds: unhappy in this life and the next

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The chapter explains its own image with “that is”: the heart is “the throne of the Lord,” that is, the place where Allah reveals Himself. “Breaking a heart” is not physical; it means hurting a person’s feelings deeply. “Both worlds” are this life and the next. “Since eternity” means from a time that has no beginning.

feedback.correct: Good. You understood the images and phrases of Chapter 10.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 10 and the poem again. Look for “that is”: it tells you what one of the images means.

languageFocusExercises.title: Situation, Interpretation and Addition
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct words for each sentence from Chapter 10.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does Yunus Emre say about love and the heart?

formChoices.sentence: According to him, where there is no love, bad feelings such as anger, heartbreak and separation [choice].
For this reason, he described breaking a heart [choice] destroying Allah’s house.
Yunus Emre emphasizes [choice] the heart but also the intellect as a value …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Where there is no X, Y appear” describes what generally happens in a situation without something; the subject “bad feelings” is plural, so the verb is “appear”. “Describe A as B” gives an interpretation of A (a learner error is “describe … like …”). “Not only … but also …” adds a second value and gives it equal weight; “both” would need “and”, and “either” would need “or”.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the forms for a general result, an interpretation and an added value.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 10 again. Check the subject of “appear”, the word that always follows “described …”, and the partner of “but also”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build the Description of the Heart
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Tap the pieces to make the sentence from Chapter 10.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does Yunus Emre describe the heart?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A “that” clause comes directly after the noun it describes: “the eye that sees the truth”. It tells us which eye the writer means. “And” then adds a second description of the heart: “the center of understanding”.

feedback.correct: Well done. The “that” clause follows the noun it describes.
feedback.incorrect: Start with “The heart is”, then name what the heart is. Put “that sees” right after the noun it describes. Check the sentence after the poem in Chapter 10.

languageFocusExercises.title: Explain Why a Value Matters
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say five or six sentences about a value, for example trust.
languageFocusExercises.question: Why does this value matter?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Useful language from the chapter includes “where there is no ..., ... appear”, “that is...”, “for this reason...”, “describe ... as ...”, “the ... that ...”, “not only ... but also ...”, and “has existed since/for ...”.

feedback.correct: Keep the paragraph connected: situation, clarification, consequence, added value, and continued importance.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Name the value: “Trust brings …”
discussionPrompts.example: Trust brings safety and peace to a friendship.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say what happens without it: “Where there is no …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Where there is no trust, problems such as doubt and jealousy appear.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Explain it: “… is …, that is, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Trust is a promise that nobody says aloud, that is, a quiet agreement between two friends.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Give a result: “For this reason, …”
discussionPrompts.example: For this reason, many people describe breaking a friend’s trust as breaking a glass that cannot be fixed.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 5–6 — Add a second value: “… value not only … but also …”
discussionPrompts.example: Good friends value not only trust but also honesty. These two values have existed in every culture for thousands of years.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: According to Yunus, what appears where there is no love?
beforeYouRead.quote: where there is no love, bad feelings such as anger, heartbreak and separation appear

iCan: I can explain why the heart matters so much for Yunus Emre.
I can explain what an image means with “that is”.
I can explain why a value matters to people.

pages.title: Intellect and Death
pages.content:
He highlights that for a person to reach salvation, heart and intellect must support one another.

He says:

[POEM]
English:
“May your intelligence / wisdom save you from all troubles
May happiness be yours for all the months and years to come”
Turkish:
Seni türlü beladan kurtara akıl,
Saadet ola sana cümle ay, yıl
[/POEM]

Death is another significant theme in Yunus’s poems. According to him, death is the best advisor for humanity, as the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) said: “Those who remember death the most and prepare best for what comes after it are the wisest.” (Ibn Majah, Zuhd, 31, no. 4259) A person who remembers the lesson of death lives a meaningful and honest life.

About death he says:

[POEM]
English:
“Whoever comes into this world must later leave it,
A guest in this world, one day they must set out for their homeland”
Turkish:
Bu dünyaya gelen kişi, ahir yine gitse gerek
Misafirdir, vatanına bir gün sefer etse gerek
[/POEM]

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
Being rescued from sin and its punishment; reaching spiritual safety.
The ability to use knowledge and experience well.
A person or thing that gives guidance.
The country or place where a person was born or truly belongs.

hotspots.title: Heart and Mind
hotspots.description: To reach salvation, the heart and the intellect must support one another.

hotspots.title: Death as an Advisor
hotspots.description: Remembering death helps a person live a meaningful and honest life.

exercises.title: Heart and Intellect
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false? Use Chapter 11.
exercises.question: In Chapter 11, Yunus Emre says that the heart and the intellect must support one another for a person to reach salvation.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11 begins: “He highlights that for a person to reach salvation, heart and intellect must support one another.” His poem also asks that “intelligence / wisdom” save a person “from all troubles.”

feedback.correct: Correct. For Yunus Emre, the heart and the intellect must work together.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first sentence of Chapter 11 and the first poem again. What do they say about the intellect?

languageFocusExercises.title: Whose Words Are These?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Who is speaking: The writer, a poem or the Prophet (pbuh)? Sort the parts.
languageFocusExercises.question: Whose words are we reading?

items: He highlights that … heart and intellect must support one another.
According to him, death is the best advisor for humanity …
“May your intelligence / wisdom save you from all troubles”
“Whoever comes into this world must later leave it”
“Those who remember death the most and prepare best for what comes after it are the wisest.”

The writer reports Yunus’s view: He highlights that … heart and intellect must support one another.
According to him, death is the best advisor for humanity …
Yunus’s own words (poem): “May your intelligence / wisdom save you from all troubles”
“Whoever comes into this world must later leave it”
The Prophet’s words: “Those who remember death the most and prepare best for what comes after it are the wisest.”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Reporting verbs and phrases such as “He highlights that …” and “According to him, …” show that the writer is telling us Yunus’s view in the writer’s own words. Quotation marks show exact words. The chapter introduces the poems with “He says:” and the saying of the Prophet with “as the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) said:”.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated reported views from exact quoted words.
feedback.incorrect: Look for quotation marks and for the words that introduce them: “He says:” or “as the Prophet … said:”. Without quotation marks, the writer is reporting the view.

languageFocusExercises.title: Say It Another Way
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 11?

transformItems.source: According to him, death is the best advisor for humanity …
transformItems.frame: He [blank] that death is the best advisor for humanity.

transformItems.source: A person who remembers the lesson of death lives a meaningful and honest life.
transformItems.frame: [blank] remembers the lesson of death lives a meaningful and honest life.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “According to + person” can be changed into a reporting verb with “that”: “He believes / says that …”. “A person who …” makes a general statement about people; “whoever” or “anyone who” says the same thing about any person who meets the condition. Note that “whoever” already contains “who”, so we do not add another “who”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the meaning with a new structure.
feedback.incorrect: For the first frame, use a reporting verb such as “believes” or “says”. For the second, think of a word that means “any person who”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Goal and Supporting Voice
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct words for each sentence from Chapter 11.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does a person need, and who said it?

formChoices.sentence: He highlights that for a person [choice] salvation, heart and intellect must support one another.
According to him, death is the best advisor for humanity, [choice] the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) said: …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “For + person + to + verb” states a goal and who has it: for a person to reach salvation. The main clause then says what is necessary for that goal: “heart and intellect must support one another”. “As + someone + said” connects a view with an earlier voice that supports it, so the reader sees that the idea has a respected source.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the goal pattern and the word that brings in a supporting voice.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first sentence of Chapter 11 and the sentence about death again. Which form follows “for a person”? Which word introduces a saying that agrees with the view?

languageFocusExercises.title: Explain a Principle and Its Consequence
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say five or six sentences about a rule for learning or friendship.
languageFocusExercises.question: What is the goal, and how can people reach it?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Useful language from the chapter includes “for a person to...”, “must...”, “According to...”, “as ... said...”, “a person who...”, and “whoever...”. Use only the patterns that fit your topic naturally.

feedback.correct: Keep the response connected: goal, necessary relationship, attributed idea, explanation, and general consequence.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give a goal: “For a student to …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: For a student to learn a new language well, regular practice is necessary.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say what must happen: “… and … must …”
discussionPrompts.example: Study at home and practice in class must support one another.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Give someone’s view: “As my teacher said, …”
discussionPrompts.example: As my English teacher said, “Small steps every day are better than one big step once a month.”

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Say why this matters: “This idea matters because …”
discussionPrompts.example: This idea matters because most students forget new words after a few days.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 5–6 — End: “A person who …” or “Whoever …”
discussionPrompts.example: A person who practises a little every day makes steady progress. Whoever waits until the night before the exam will find it very hard.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: In the first poem, what can save you from all troubles?
beforeYouRead.quote: May your intelligence / wisdom save you from all troubles

I can tell apart a reported view and someone’s exact words.
I can explain a principle and its result for people in general.

pages.title: Morality and Good Habits
pages.content:
Yunus believes that true morality is about giving up bad habits that are not suitable for people. Moral rules such as honesty, patience, humility, generosity, respect, trust in Allah, and modesty are important in Yunus Emre’s works. With these principles, Yunus Emre teaches people the path to an honest life. He also taught people to avoid bad habits like being arrogant, stingy, greedy, selfish, or jealous, and gossiping.

Yunus Emre’s poems are not only literary works but also a moral guide.

Here are some of his verses about morality:

Yunus says:

[POEM]
English:
“I’ve fallen into the prison of greed and cannot escape
It’s a hard, rock-solid place; I cannot break free”
Turkish:
Tamah hapsine düştüm çıkamam
Katı berktir duvarı yıkamam
[/POEM]

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
Principles about right and wrong behavior.
The quality of not thinking you are better than others.
The willingness to give and help others.
A strong selfish desire for more wealth or possessions.
Being shy and decent, and not showing off.

hotspots.title: Morality
hotspots.description: True morality means giving up bad habits that do not suit people.

hotspots.title: Good Habits
hotspots.description: Yunus praised honesty, patience, humility, generosity, respect, trust in Allah and modesty.

exercises.title: The Prison of Greed
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the best answer from Chapter 12.
exercises.question: In the poem in Chapter 12, what does “the prison of greed” show?
options: Greed keeps a person safe, like strong walls around a house.
Greed traps a person, and it is very hard to break free from it.
Yunus Emre was put in a real prison because of gossiping.
exercises.explanation: The poem begins “I’ve fallen into the prison of greed and cannot escape” and goes on: “It’s a hard, rock-solid place; I cannot break free”. Greed is one of the bad habits Yunus teaches people to avoid.

feedback.correct: Right. The prison is an image: Greed holds a person like hard walls, so it is wiser not to fall into it.
feedback.incorrect: Read the two lines of the poem at the end of Chapter 12 again. Think about what a prison does to the person inside it.

languageFocusExercises.title: Principles and Bad Habits
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Is it a good habit to build, or a bad habit to avoid? Sort the words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which habits are good, and which are bad?

items: honesty
patience
humility
generosity
arrogant
stingy
greedy
jealous

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The principles are nouns that name qualities: honesty, patience, humility, generosity. The bad habits are adjectives that describe people, so the chapter puts them after “being”: “bad habits like being arrogant, stingy, greedy …”. Many pairs are related: generous → generosity, humble → humility, patient → patience, honest → honesty.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated the principles (nouns) from the bad habits (adjectives).
feedback.incorrect: Look at the first paragraph of Chapter 12. Which words come after “such as”, and which come after “like being”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Define, Give Examples, Guide
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 12 with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which word fits each gap?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: Yunus believes that true morality is about [blank] up bad habits that are not suitable for people. Moral rules [blank] as honesty, patience, humility, generosity, respect, trust in Allah, and modesty are important in Yunus Emre’s works. … He also taught people [blank] avoid bad habits like [blank] arrogant, stingy, greedy, selfish, or jealous, and gossiping.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “About” is a preposition, so it is followed by an -ing form: “is about giving up”. “Such as” introduces examples of a larger group. “Teach + person + to + verb” shows guidance toward an action. “Like” is also a preposition here, so the verb after it takes -ing: “like being arrogant”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used -ing after prepositions and “to + verb” after “teach people”.
feedback.incorrect: Check the first paragraph of Chapter 12. Remember: after a preposition (about, like) we use -ing.

languageFocusExercises.title: Find and Fix the Mistake
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about Yunus Emre’s poems?

errorItems.sentence: With these principles, Yunus Emre teach people the path to an honest life.
Yunus Emre’s poems are not only literary works and also a moral guide.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “With these principles” shows the means: The principles are what Yunus uses to guide people. The subject “Yunus Emre” is singular, so the present simple verb takes -s: “teaches”. “Not only … but also …” is a fixed pair: It adds a second role (a moral guide) and gives it the same importance as the first (literary works).

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the verb and completed the fixed pair.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 12 again. Is “Yunus Emre” one person or many? Which word always goes with “not only … also”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Define a Value and Turn It into Action
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say five or six sentences about a value, for example respect.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does the value mean, and how do we show it?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Useful language from the chapter includes “is about + -ing”, “such as...”, “with these principles...”, “teach someone to...”, “avoid...”, and “not only... but also...”. Use only the forms that fit your topic naturally.

feedback.correct: Keep the response connected: definition, examples, guidance, contrast in behavior, and a wider role or result.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Explain the value: “Respect is about …ing …”
discussionPrompts.example: Respect is about listening to others and treating them fairly.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Give examples: “… such as …, … and …”
discussionPrompts.example: We show respect in small ways, such as waiting our turn, saying thank you and using kind words.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Say how it guides us: “Our teacher teaches us to …”
discussionPrompts.example: Our teacher teaches us to listen to classmates without interrupting them.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Compare: “We should …, and we should avoid …”
discussionPrompts.example: We should praise our classmates’ good ideas, and we should avoid laughing at their mistakes.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 5–6 — End: “… is not only … but also …”
discussionPrompts.example: Respect is not only good for friendships but also good for learning. In a respectful class, everyone feels safe to ask questions.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What is true morality about?
beforeYouRead.quote: true morality is about giving up bad habits

iCan: I can name the good habits and bad habits in the chapter.
I can give examples and say what someone teaches others to do.
I can turn a value into clear actions.

pages.title: A Moral Guide
pages.content:
In another verse, he talks about “patience” and says:

[POEM]
English:
“Patience is the foundation of an everlasting kingdom,
And those who are blessed with patience will reach greatness.”
Turkish:
Sabırlu devleti dâim olur
Nasibi sabır olanlar ulu olur
[/POEM]

[POEM]
English:
“Whoever possesses patience rises to the heavens,
For within patience lies every kind of skill”
Turkish:
Sabır kimde ise o arşa yükselir
Ki sabrın içinde bulunur türlü hünerler
[/POEM]

In the following verse, he warns against “rage and arrogance”:

[POEM]
English:
“Whoever is filled with anger loses their faith
If faith is required, one must give up rage”
Turkish:
Buşu kimde ise imanı gider
İman gerek ise öfkeyi gider
[/POEM]

It is clear that Yunus Emre was an important person of his era, and his poems are still valuable today as a moral guide for future generations.

His works are as follows:

Risalat al-Nushiyya (a book of moral advice)

Divan (his collected poems)

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:yunus-yunus-emre
The ability to stay calm and continue through difficulty.
Tells people about a danger so that they can avoid it.
Very strong anger.
The belief that you are better or more important than others.
The base that something stands on.
Never ending.
To have.

hotspots.title: Lasting Value
hotspots.description: His poems are still valuable today as a moral guide for future generations.

hotspots.title: Patience
hotspots.description: His verses praise patience and warn against rage and arrogance.

exercises.title: A Moral Guide
exercises.instructions: Match each word or title with what Chapter 13 says about it.
exercises.question: What does Chapter 13 say about each of these?

matchingPairs.right: the foundation of an everlasting kingdom
makes the person it fills lose their faith
a book of moral advice
Yunus Emre’s collected poems

correctAnswer.Patience: the foundation of an everlasting kingdom
correctAnswer.Anger: makes the person it fills lose their faith

exercises.explanation: The verses say “Patience is the foundation of an everlasting kingdom” and “Whoever is filled with anger loses their faith.” The chapter names his works: Risalat al-Nushiyya (a book of moral advice) and Divan (his collected poems).

feedback.correct: Well done. Yunus praises patience, warns against anger, and his works still guide people today.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the three poems first, then at the list of his works at the end of Chapter 13.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Do the Lines Mean?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each line from the poems in Chapter 13 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do the lines say about patience and anger?

matchingPairs.left: Patience is the foundation of an everlasting kingdom
matchingPairs.right: Success that lasts is built on patience.

matchingPairs.left: those who are blessed with patience will reach greatness
matchingPairs.right: People given the gift of patience will one day become great.

matchingPairs.left: Whoever possesses patience rises to the heavens
matchingPairs.right: Any patient person reaches a very high spiritual place.

matchingPairs.left: Whoever is filled with anger loses their faith
matchingPairs.right: A person full of anger has their belief taken away.

matchingPairs.left: If faith is required, one must give up rage
matchingPairs.right: To keep your belief, you have to leave anger behind.

correctAnswer.Patience is the foundation of an everlas: Success that lasts is built on patience.
correctAnswer.those who are blessed with patience will: People given the gift of patience will one day become great.
correctAnswer.Whoever possesses patience rises to the: Any patient person reaches a very high spiritual place.
correctAnswer.Whoever is filled with anger loses their: A person full of anger has their belief taken away.
correctAnswer.If faith is required, one must give up r: To keep your belief, you have to leave anger behind.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The lines use patterns that turn one observation into a general principle. “Those who … will …” links a group of people with a future result. “Whoever …” means any person who meets the condition. “If …, one must …” gives a condition and then a strong general duty; “one” means any person, not one particular person.

feedback.correct: Good. You understood the meaning of each line.
feedback.incorrect: Read the poems in Chapter 13 again. Which line gives a future result, which gives a condition and a duty, and which describe what happens to any patient or angry person?

languageFocusExercises.title: Who Is “One”?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the line from the poem in Chapter 13. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “If faith is required, one must give up rage” Who does “one” refer to in this line?
options: one particular person that Yunus is speaking to
Yunus Emre himself and nobody else
the first person in a list
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “One” can be an impersonal pronoun meaning “any person” or “people in general”. With “must”, it gives advice that is true for everybody, not for one named person. In everyday English we often say “you” with the same meaning: “If you want to keep your faith, you must give up rage.”

feedback.correct: Correct. “One must …” gives a general duty for any person.
feedback.incorrect: Read the whole line again. Does the poem name a person, or does it give advice that applies to everyone?

languageFocusExercises.title: Linking the Verses
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 13 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which word fits each gap?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: [blank] another verse, he talks about “patience” and says: … In the following verse, he warns [blank] “rage and arrogance”: … It is clear that Yunus Emre was an important person of his era, and his poems are [blank] valuable today as a moral guide for future generations. His works are as [blank]:
languageFocusExercises.explanation: We say “in a verse” (like “in a poem”, “in a book”). “Warn against + noun” names the danger someone tells us to avoid. “Still” shows that something from the past continues now: The poems were valuable then and are valuable today. “As follows:” is a fixed phrase that introduces a list.

feedback.correct: Well done. You linked the verses and brought the poems into the present.
feedback.incorrect: Read the lines between the poems and the last paragraph of Chapter 13 again. Which preposition goes with “verse”? Which fixed phrase introduces a list?

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Short Principle-and-Result Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say five sentences about a good rule for life, for example patience.
languageFocusExercises.question: Why is this rule important?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Useful language from the chapter includes “those who ... will ...”, “whoever ...”, “if ...”, “one must ...”, and a transition such as “in another case” or “in the following example”. Use only the forms that fit your message naturally.

feedback.correct: Keep the response connected: principle, general condition, consequence, related warning or example, and final guidance.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give the rule and why it matters.
discussionPrompts.example: Patience is important when you learn a musical instrument because progress is slow.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say who wins: “Those who … will …”
discussionPrompts.example: Those who practise patiently will play beautiful music one day.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Say more: “Whoever …”
discussionPrompts.example: Whoever keeps trying after a mistake becomes stronger and more confident.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Add a warning: “In the same way, …”
discussionPrompts.example: In the same way, anger can stop your progress because angry learners often give up.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 5 — End with advice: “If one wants to …, one must …”
discussionPrompts.example: If one wants to play well, one must accept small mistakes and keep going.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What does Yunus warn against in the last verse?

iCan: I can explain what Yunus Emre’s verses say about patience and anger.
I can make general statements about any person with “whoever” and “one”.
I can write a short paragraph with a principle and its result.

groupTask.title: A Guide in Simple Words

roles.name: Quote Finder
roles.job: You choose one principle from Chapters 12–13 and copy one line about it exactly as the book writes it.

roles.name: Meaning Explainer

roles.name: Designer and Presenter

steps: Choose one principle: patience, honesty or controlling anger.

legend.seljuk-pressure: Anatolian Seljuk lands under Mongol pressure

age.born: Yunus Emre is born around this time.
age.died: Yunus Emre dies around this time. He is about {years} old.

places.name: Anatolia
places.text: Yunus Emre was a famous Turkish poet and a Sufi from Anatolia. He was born around 1240–1241 and died around 1320–1321. He lived in a very difficult time, but he traveled around Anatolia as a wise dervish and helped people with his poetry.
places.teacherNote: The book names no birthplace, lodge or grave, so the map shows only the region. Chapter 4: the Anatolian Seljuk Sultan Ala al-Din Kayqubad I (1220–1237) built a navy in the Mediterranean and Black Seas; point to both sea names. The line from the east shows people migrating to Anatolia from Central Asia because of the Mongol invasion (Chapter 4); its path is approximate.
places.question: Why was Yunus Emre’s time a very difficult time in Anatolia?

places.name: Erzurum, 1242
places.text: In 1242, the Mongols from Azerbaijan captured Erzurum and killed its people. This disaster caused deep sorrow and fear among the people of the Anatolian Seljuks.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 5. The book does not describe the Mongols’ road; the army line from Azerbaijan to Erzurum is approximate.
places.question: How did people feel after the Mongols captured Erzurum?

places.name: Kösedağ, 1243
places.text: In 1243, the Anatolian Seljuk army and the Mongols clashed at Kösedağ, 80 km northeast of Sivas. The Mongols used a false retreat and then circled the army, so they won easily. After that, they destroyed and raided Sivas, Kayseri and Erzincan.
places.teacherNote: The book gives the place as 80 km northeast of Sivas; the exact battlefield is not known, so the pin is approximate. Chapter 3 says this defeat caused the Mongols’ invasion of Anatolia. Chapter 6 continues: Men were killed, women and children were taken captive, and the cities were deserted.
places.question: Which three cities did the Mongols raid after the battle? Find them on the map.

places.name: Azerbaijan
places.text: In Yunus Emre’s time, there were Mongols in Azerbaijan. The Babai revolts made the Anatolian Seljuks weak, and this gave these Mongols the courage to attack them.
places.teacherNote: Medieval Azerbaijan was the land around Tabriz, mostly in north-west Iran today. It is not the same as the modern Republic of Azerbaijan. The pin is approximate.
places.question: What gave the Mongols in Azerbaijan the courage to attack?

places.name: Iran
places.text: The Ilkhanate Empire was the Mongol state centred in Iran. After 1277, the Mongols ruled Anatolia through the commanders and governors that they sent. In 1308, the lands of Anatolia were directly attached to the Ilkhanate Empire. Under Mongol pressure, shaykhs from Turkestan, Khorasan and Iran came to Anatolia.
places.teacherNote: The book does not say where the commanders and governors came from; the light from Iran only shows Mongol rule reaching Anatolia. The pin marks Iran as a region, not a city. Turkestan and Khorasan are farther east, off this map.
places.question: What changed in Anatolia in 1308?

challenge.prompt: Find Anatolia, the land where Yunus Emre lived and recited his verses.
Find Kösedağ. It is 80 km northeast of Sivas.
Find Erzurum. The Mongols captured it in 1242.
Find Kayseri. The Mongols raided it after the battle of Kösedağ.
Find Azerbaijan. The Mongols who attacked the Anatolian Seljuks were there.

pages.title: Knowledge Check
pages.content: Check your understanding of the complete B1 story.

exercises.title: Plain Words
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 2.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 2, how does Yunus Emre’s plain language help people?
options: It helps them understand his writings easily.
It teaches them Arabic, Persian and Islamic sciences.
It brings people together in the tekkes of Anatolia.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “This plain language helps people understand his writings and sayings easily.”

feedback.correct: Correct. His language is simple and clear, so people can understand his writings and sayings without difficulty.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the first paragraph of Chapter 2. What does the plain language help people do?

exercises.title: Support for the Tekkes
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 3, government officials supported the tekkes.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “Furthermore, they received support from government officials.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. Tekkes helped people and brought them together, and government officials supported them.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the first paragraph of Chapter 3. Who supported the tekkes?

exercises.title: A Brilliant Period
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 4.
exercises.question: Why does Chapter 4 call the rule of Ala al-Din Kayqubad I the most powerful period of the Seljuks?
options: He defeated the Mongols in the battle at Kösedağ.
He expanded the borders and built a navy in two seas.
He managed the growing Turkmen population well.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “He expanded the country’s borders and established a navy in the Mediterranean and Black Seas.”

feedback.correct: Correct. He made the country larger and built a navy in the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, so the Seljuks became the strongest state in the Middle East.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the second paragraph of Chapter 4. What did Ala al-Din Kayqubad I do during his rule?

exercises.title: A Chance for the Mongols
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 5.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 5, what gave the Mongols in Azerbaijan the courage to attack the Seljuks?
options: The Seljuk army had lost its navy in the Black Sea.
The people of Erzurum had asked them for help.
The Seljuks had just ended a revolt with great difficulty.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5: “In the end, the Seljuk forces put an end to the rebellion with great difficulty and defeated the rebels with swords.” Chapter 5: “However, this situation gave the Mongols in Azerbaijan the courage to attack the Seljuk Empire.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The hard fight against the rebels showed that the Seljuk state was weak, and the Mongols saw their chance.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the end of the first paragraph of Chapter 5 and the sentence that follows it. What does “this situation” refer to?

exercises.title: Mongol Governors
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 6, after 1277 the Mongols governed Anatolia through commanders and governors they sent.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6: “After 1277, the Mongols began to administer Anatolia through the commanders and governors that they sent.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. The Seljuk sultans lost more and more power, and the Mongols sent their own commanders and governors.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the last part of Chapter 6. What happened in Anatolia after 1277?

exercises.title: The Dervishes
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 7.
exercises.question: Why were the dervishes trained by the shaykhs important, according to Chapter 7?
options: They sent the state’s income to the Mongols every year.
They spread a simple understanding of Islam among nomads.
They fought against the Mongols in Anatolia’s cities.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7: “These dervishes were influential among nomads.” Chapter 7: “They were spreading a simple understanding of Islam and establishing popular Sufism.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The dervishes had influence among nomads and spread a simple form of Islam and popular Sufism.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the first paragraph of Chapter 7. Among whom were the dervishes influential, and what did they spread?

exercises.title: A Guest in This World
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 11.
exercises.question: In the poem about death in Chapter 11, a person is called a “guest.” What does this show?
options: A person stays in this world only for a while.
A person should travel around Anatolia like Yunus.
A person is always welcome at the tekke.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11: “Whoever comes into this world must later leave it,” Chapter 11: “A guest in this world, one day they must set out for their homeland”

feedback.correct: Correct. A guest does not stay forever. In the same way, every person who comes into this world must leave it one day.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the last poem of Chapter 11. What must everyone who comes into this world do later?

exercises.title: More Than Poems
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 12, Yunus Emre’s poems are only literary works, not a guide for life.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 12: “Yunus Emre’s poems are not only literary works but also a moral guide.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. His poems are literature, and they also teach people how to live an honest life.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the short paragraph in the middle of Chapter 12. What else are his poems besides literary works?

pages.title: Master Glossary
pages.content: Review all key vocabulary from the story in one place.

vocabulary.definition: Belonging to the part that people can see.
vocabulary.storyExample: Sufis lead a way of life within the outer (visible) and inner rules of Islam.

vocabulary.definition: Unfair opinions or preferences about people.
vocabulary.storyExample: They expect nothing in return and do good to everyone without biases.

vocabulary.definition: To say a poem or a text aloud, often from memory.
vocabulary.storyExample: In addition to being a Sufi, Yunus Emre was one of the first to write and recite poems in simple Turkish.

vocabulary.definition: Connected with the writing of poems, stories and other artistic works.
vocabulary.storyExample: The words and phrases which he used helped develop a better literary Turkish.

vocabulary.definition: Simple, clear and easy to understand.
vocabulary.storyExample: This plain language helps people understand his writings and sayings easily.

vocabulary.definition: A particular period of history.
vocabulary.storyExample: According to historical sources, he lived during the same era as important people like Haji Bektash Veli and Mevlana Jalal al-Din Rumi.

vocabulary.definition: Books, documents or people that give information, especially about the past.
vocabulary.storyExample: According to historical sources, he lived during the same era as important people like Haji Bektash Veli and Mevlana Jalal al-Din Rumi.

vocabulary.definition: A teacher who guides and teaches one person or a small group.
vocabulary.storyExample: But he also studied Allah’s love and morals at the tekke, which was a place where Sufi education was taught under the guidance of a sheikh (spiritual tutor).

vocabulary.definition: Organized actions in which people fight against their rulers.
vocabulary.storyExample: The Anatolian Seljuks were seriously weakened by the Babai revolts in the 13th century.

vocabulary.definition: The act of entering another country by force to take control of it.
vocabulary.storyExample: The defeat caused the Mongols' invasion of Anatolia.

vocabulary.definition: The conditions that affect a situation or a person’s life.
vocabulary.storyExample: Because of these hard circumstances, Anatolia faced serious political, economic, and social problems.

vocabulary.definition: Trying very hard to deal with something difficult.
vocabulary.storyExample: People were struggling to cope with these tough situations.

vocabulary.definition: A country’s military force that operates at sea.

pages.content: Retrieve the book through sequencing, matching, reflection, and the Review Quiz.

exercises.title: Notice: Who Is in Focus?
exercises.instructions: Do we learn who did the action? Put each sentence in the right group.
exercises.question: When does the book say who did it?

dragDropGroups.group: Active: The subject does the action
items: He expanded the country’s borders and established a navy …
The Mongols used the classic false retreat and circling tactic.
These shaykhs trained dervishes in their teachings.

dragDropGroups.group: Passive with “by”: the doer is named at the end
items: The Anatolian Seljuks were seriously weakened by the Babai revolts …
He was also inspired by the ideas and experiences of earlier Muslim Sufis.

dragDropGroups.group: Passive without a doer: Who did it is not said
items: Yunus Emre is known as one of the founders of Turkish Sufi literature.
… Sufi education was taught under the guidance of a sheikh …
Finally, an agreement was made with the Mongols …

Active: The subject does the action: He expanded the country’s borders and established a navy …
The Mongols used the classic false retreat and circling tactic.
These shaykhs trained dervishes in their teachings.
Passive with “by”: the doer is named at: The Anatolian Seljuks were seriously weakened by the Babai revolts …
He was also inspired by the ideas and experiences of earlier Muslim Sufis.
Passive without a doer: Who did it is no: Yunus Emre is known as one of the founders of Turkish Sufi literature.
… Sufi education was taught under the guidance of a sheikh …
Finally, an agreement was made with the Mongols …

exercises.explanation: In an active sentence the subject acts: Ala al-Din Kayqubad I expanded, the Mongols used, the shaykhs trained. The passive (be + past participle) puts the person or thing that the action happens to in first position: The Seljuks were weakened, Yunus was inspired. The writer adds “by + doer” only when the doer matters (the Babai revolts, earlier Sufis). When the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant, it is left out: is known, was taught, was made. The focus is on the result, not on who did it.

feedback.correct: Well done. You separated active sentences, passives with “by” and passives without a doer.
feedback.incorrect: First find the verb. Is it be + past participle (were weakened, is known)? Then look for “by”: Does the sentence name who did it? Check Chapters 1–7.

exercises.title: Notice: How Sure Is the Writer?
exercises.instructions: Read the sentences from the book. Then choose the best answer.
exercises.question: “He was born around 1240–1241 …” / “Some sources say that he received a good madrasa education …” / “According to Yunus Emre, Allah, the Creator, is the source of all things.” / “He highlights that for a person to reach salvation, heart and intellect must support one another.” What do “around”, “Some sources say that”, “According to” and “He highlights that” do in these sentences?
options: They show that the writer thinks this information is false.
They show where an idea comes from, or that a fact is not exact.
They give the reason why each of these events happened.
They show that these things happened again and again.
exercises.explanation: A careful writer shows how sure a piece of information is and whose idea it is. “Around” gives an approximate date. “Some sources say that …” reports what only part of the evidence says. “According to + person” and a reporting verb such as “He highlights that …” give the idea to its owner: It is Yunus Emre’s view, reported by the writer. None of these phrases says the information is false; they make the claim exact and honest.

feedback.correct: Correct. These phrases show the source of an idea and how certain it is.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the words before each idea: around, some sources, according to, he highlights. Do they give a reason, or do they show whose idea it is and how sure it is?

exercises.title: Notice: Not Only … But Also
exercises.instructions: Read the sentences from the book. Is the statement true or false?
exercises.question: Chapter 3: “At that time, tekkes were not only places for Sufi training. They were also important community organizations …” Chapter 10: “Yunus Emre emphasizes not only the heart but also the intellect as a value …” Chapter 12: “Yunus Emre’s poems are not only literary works but also a moral guide.” Statement: In these sentences, the second idea replaces the first one. For example, Yunus Emre’s poems are a moral guide, not literary works.
exercises.explanation: ‘Not only A but also B’ keeps A and adds B with the same weight: The poems are literary works AND a moral guide; Yunus values the heart AND the intellect. In Chapter 3 the pattern is split over two sentences: “not only …” in the first, “also …” in the second. The pattern is used when the second point might surprise the reader.

feedback.correct: Correct. Nothing is replaced: “not only … but also …” adds a second point to the first.
feedback.incorrect: Read the Chapter 12 sentence again. Does it say the poems are not literary works, or that they are literary works and something more?

exercises.title: Build: Reason, Turn and Result
exercises.instructions: Complete the lines from the book with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
exercises.question: Which word fits each gap?
exercises.fillBlanksText: People love his works very much [blank] his style. … At the time of his death, the Seljuks were the most powerful and largest state in the Middle East. [blank], his son Kaykhusraw II (1237–1246) did not rule the country well, so Seljuk money and social life began to get worse. The Mongol invasion [blank] many people to migrate to Anatolia from Central Asia … It is “the throne of the Lord,” that is, the place where Allah reveals Himself. [blank], he described breaking a heart as destroying Allah’s house.
exercises.explanation: “Due to” and “because of” are followed by a noun (due to his style); “because” needs a clause with a subject and a verb. “However” turns the story: After the strongest period, things get worse. “Cause + object + to + verb” shows what an event led people to do (caused many people to migrate); “made” would need a verb without “to”. “For this reason” points back to the idea before it and gives its result: The heart is where Allah reveals Himself, so breaking a heart is very serious.

feedback.correct: Well done. You linked reasons, a turn and results across the book.
feedback.incorrect: At each gap, ask: Is a noun or a clause next? Does the story turn, or does a result follow? Check Chapter 2, the middle of Chapter 4 and Chapter 10.

exercises.title: Build: What Comes Next?
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct form for each sentence from the book.
exercises.question: Which form comes after “helped”, “failure” and “for”?

formChoices.sentence: The words and phrases which he used helped [choice] a better literary Turkish.
… Kaykhusraw II’s failure [choice] this situation worsened the social and economic chaos.
His words remind us of Allah’s commands for [choice] this unity.

exercises.explanation: After “help” (or “help + person”), we use the base verb: helped develop (Chapter 1); “help to + verb” is also possible, but never -ing or a past form. Some nouns are followed by “to + verb”: failure to manage (Chapter 4), just like the verb ‘fail to manage’. After a preposition such as “for”, “without” or “about”, a verb takes the -ing form: for achieving (Chapter 9).

feedback.correct: Correct. Help + base verb; failure + to + verb; preposition + -ing.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the word just before the gap. Is it “helped”, the noun “failure” or the preposition “for”? Check Chapters 1, 4 and 9.

exercises.title: Build: Fix the History Verbs

errorItems.sentence: They followed spiritual leaders called 'Baba' because they believed these leaders will save them.
The women and children were took captive and forced to go with the Mongols.

exercises.explanation: “Was/were + -ing” describes a situation that was going on in the background: Anatolia was experiencing total chaos (Chapter 7). After a past verb like “believed”, “would + base verb” shows what people expected at that time; it does not say that it really happened (Chapter 5). The passive needs “be + past participle”: were taken, not were took (Chapter 6).

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected all three verbs.
feedback.incorrect: Ask for each sentence: is it a background situation (was + -ing), an expectation in the past (would + verb), or a passive (were + past participle)? Check Chapters 5, 6 and 7.

exercises.title: Build: Say It Another Way

transformItems.source: The rule of the Anatolian Seljuk Sultan Ala al-Din Kayqubad I (1220–1237) was the most powerful and brilliant period of the Seljuks.
transformItems.frame: No other period of the Seljuks was as [blank] as the rule of Ala al-Din Kayqubad I.

exercises.explanation: A superlative (“the most powerful and brilliant”) can be said with a negative comparison: ‘No other period was as powerful and brilliant as …’ (Chapter 4). “Where” (or “in which”) begins a clause about a place: ‘places where poets improved their skills’ (Chapter 3). In a general statement the verb agrees with the person: “a person who lives …”, but ‘people who live …’ (Chapter 11).

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the meaning and changed the structure.
feedback.incorrect: Keep the meaning of the book sentence. Ask: Which comparison keeps “the most”? Which word begins a clause about a place? Is the subject one person or many people?

exercises.title: Use: Our New School Library
exercises.instructions: Complete this new text with words from the bank. Three words are extra.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s words to tell about your school?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Two years ago, our school library was a small, dark room next to the gym. Very few students went there [blank] the noise from the gym. [blank], last summer the library was moved to a bright room on the first floor. New shelves were built there. Many new books [blank] by families from our town, too. According to our librarian, Mrs Selin, the number of visitors has doubled this year. The new library is not only quieter [blank] more comfortable. Now students read there during their breaks, and some of them help younger children choose books.
exercises.explanation: “Due to + noun” gives the reason (the noise). “However” turns the text from the problem to the change. “Were donated” is passive: The books are in focus, and “by families” names the doer. “According to our librarian” shows whose information it is. “Not only … but also …” adds a second quality with the same weight. Like the book, the text reports a change carefully and clearly.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s language to report a change in a new place.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask: A noun or a clause after it? A turn in the story? Who is in focus: The books or the families? Which words complete “not only …”?

exercises.title: Use: Check a Classmate’s Sentences
exercises.instructions: Each sentence from a classmate has one mistake. Tap it and choose the correct words.

errorItems.sentence: Our class trip was cancel yesterday, so we stayed at school.

exercises.explanation: The passive needs a past participle: “was cancelled”. “Because of” is followed by a noun (the bad weather); “because” needs a subject and a verb. “Whoever” means “any person who”, so the verb is singular: “Whoever wants to join …”.

feedback.correct: Well done. Your classmate’s sentences are now correct.
feedback.incorrect: Ask for each sentence: be + past participle? a noun or a clause after “because”? one person or many after “whoever”?

exercises.title: Use: A Change in Our Community
exercises.instructions: Write 5–6 sentences about a real change in your school or town.
exercises.question: Can you tell the news of a change clearly?
exercises.explanation: Example: “Three years ago, the park in our neighbourhood was full of rubbish, and few families were using it. However, last spring the park was cleaned by volunteers from our school, and new benches were put in. According to my neighbor, Mr Hasan, more children play there now than ever before. The park is not only cleaner but also safer because it has new lights. For this reason, my friends and I go there almost every day. Anyone who uses the park should help keep it clean.”

feedback.correct: Check your paragraph: was/were + -ing for the background; However for the turn; was/were + past participle for the change; According to … for someone’s view; not only … but also …; because / because of, For this reason; Anyone who … should ….

options: Because death takes away the need to work.
Because only old people should think about death.
Because remembering death helps a person live honestly.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11 says: “According to him, death is the best advisor for humanity” and “A person who remembers the lesson of death lives a meaningful and honest life.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Remembering death guides a person to live a meaningful and honest life.
feedback.incorrect: Read the paragraph about death in Chapter 11. What kind of life does it lead to?

exercises.title: Yunus and His Times
exercises.instructions: Put these events in the order they happened.
exercises.question: How do Yunus Emre’s life and the history of Anatolia fit together?

sequencingItems.text: The Mongols defeat the Seljuks at Kösedağ.
The rule of Sultan Ala al-Din Kayqubad I ends.
Anatolia is attached to the Ilkhanate.

exercises.explanation: Ala al-Din Kayqubad I ruled until 1237 (Chapter 4). Yunus was born around 1240–1241 (Chapter 2). Kösedağ was in 1243 (Chapter 5). Anatolia was attached to the Ilkhanate in 1308 (Chapter 6). Yunus died around 1320–1321 (Chapter 2).

feedback.correct: Yes. Yunus was a small child at Kösedağ and lived through the whole Mongol period.
feedback.incorrect: Use the dates in Chapters 2, 4, 5 and 6.
